extracted.subtask_description: A set of focused creative-writing exercises and guidelines for practicing point-of-view shifts, dialogue-only scenes, indirect description/implication, and integrating exposition without lumps. Includes instructions, constraints (word counts, voices), and critiquing pointers useful in workshops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking revisions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark the changes with line breaks, with the narrator’s name in parentheses at the head of that section, or with any device you like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or circulating drafts that experiment with multiple narrators/POVs, make the changes visible to readers or workshop participants using line breaks, narrator labels, or another clear device so readers can track structural shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shifting POV is risky but teachable (Thin Ice)
rubrics_metrics.description: I keep saying that shifting POV frequently and without notice is risky, dangerous. So you want to do something dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (Thin Ice): In 300–1000 words, tell the same or a new story deliberately shifting POV from character to character several times without any obvious signal to the reader. This calls for a different narrative technique (likely an involved author voice) and you will learn by doing, but be aware the technique is dangerous — the 'ice really is thin, and the waters are deep.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal POV transitions subtly but clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice how Woolf makes the transitions effortlessly but perfectly clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete signals for shifts: physical actions or details seen by a particular character (e.g., 'pursing her lips'), paragraph indentation, changes in perception or focalization. Transitions should be effortless to the reader yet provide enough cue (sensory detail, action, focalized thought) to identify the new viewpoint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique POV shifting on effectiveness and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: In critiquing these exercises, you might talk about how well the shifts work, what's gained (or lost?) by them, how the piece might have differed if told from one POV only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workshop discussion should address clarity of shifts, narrative advantages/disadvantages, and hypothetical single-POV alternatives — does shifting add depth, confusion, intimacy, distance?

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as conscious practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conscious, deliberate imitation of a piece of prose one admires can be good training, a means toward finding one’s own voice as a narrative writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you imitate an example, treat it as practice: be conscious (not plagiaristic), and remember the exercise is to develop skill and freedom in your own voice, not to produce a finished piece for publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue-only scene (A & B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The goal of this exercise is to tell a story and present two characters through dialogue alone. Write a page or two of pure dialogue, like a play, with A and B as the characters' names. No stage directions. No description of the characters. Nothing but what A says and what B says.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All information about who they are, where they are, and what's going on must come through what they say. Suggested topics: crisis situations (car out of gas, spaceship about to crash, doctor recognizes patient as parent, etc.). Note: this is an exercise in one element of storytelling rather than a short story form to be overused in prose fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiquing dialogue-only pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: If the text's clear enough for another person to read, when reading it aloud, it's good fun. In discussing or thinking about it, consider: Is the story clear? Do we learn enough about the people and the situation—do we need more information? Or less? What do we in fact know about the people (for example, do we know their gender)? What do we feel about them? Could we tell the two voices apart without the A and B signals, and if not, how might they be more differentiated? Do people actually talk this way?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read aloud (author and others) to detect stumbling, mis-emphasis, stagy vs natural speech. Use such readings to locate where voices need differentiation or where implied information is insufficient or excessive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyphony / letting characters have distinct voices
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the marvelous things about the novel is its many-voicedness, its polyphony. All kinds of people get to think, feel, and talk in a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using characters as mouthpieces for the author. Practice listening and sinking self into character-self so voices arise from the character. If you are a fiction writer: 'Listen. Just be quiet, and listen. Let the character talk. Don't censor, don't control. Listen, and write.' You can always delete later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being the Stranger exercise (single viewpoint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a narrative of 200–600 words, a scene involving at least two people and some kind of action or event. Use a single viewpoint character, in either first person or limited third person, who is involved in the event. Give us the character's thoughts and feelings in their own words. The viewpoint character is to be somebody you dislike, or disapprove of, or hate, or feel to be extremely different from yourself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological difference is the aim; stick close to home rather than invent across unfamiliar cultures/languages. Try changing gender, age, or the usual vantage (child vs parent). Memoirists can invent for fiction; fiction writers can make it memoir-like. Avoid using it as therapy; it's an exercise in psychological displacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiquing 'Being the Stranger' — inside viewpoint vs author judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: In critiquing, you might use this last suggestion as a criterion. As readers, are we really inside the viewpoint character, so that we understand something about how they see the world, or did the writer stay outside, sitting in judgment, trying to force us to make the same judgment? If there's spitefulness, vindictiveness, in the piece, whose is it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether voice convinces or rings false/true; identify moments where writerial judgment leaks in; discuss whether the exercise succeeded in suspending the author's moral/emotional stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication: character by indirection and the untold event
rubrics_metrics.description: Each part should involve 200–600 words of descriptive prose. In both, the voice is either involved author or detached author. No viewpoint character. Character by indirection: Describe a character by describing any place inhabited or frequented by that character (the character isn't present). The untold event: Give us a glimpse of the mood and nature of some event or deed by describing the place where it happened or is about to happen (the event doesn't happen in your piece). You aren't to say anything directly about the person or the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use props, furniture, clothes, belongings, weather, plants, smells, sounds — any detail that reveals character or suggests action. Build up evidence into a consistent, coherent mood or atmosphere from which readers can infer the absent person or untold act. Avoid mere inventories; every detail must tell.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory guidance and voice constraints (detached vs involved)
rubrics_metrics.description: In descriptive writing, give a thought from time to time to the senses other than sight. Sound, above all, is evocative. We have a limited vocabulary for smell, but mention of a certain scent or stink can set a feeling-tone. Taste and touch are forbidden to the detached author. The involved author can go around telling us how things feel to the hand, though I don't think even an involved author gets to actually eat the fruit...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose authorial voice (detached or involved) deliberately and apply sensory limits accordingly: detached = no taste/touch claims; involved = may describe tactile sensations and implied taste, but be judicious. Use sound and smell to strengthen implication and atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the Expository Lump
rubrics_metrics.description: If the information is poured out as a lecture, barely concealed by some stupid device — 'Oh, Captain, do tell me how the antimatter dissimulator works!' and then he does, endlessly — we have what science fiction writers call an Expository Lump. Crafty writers (in any genre) don't allow Exposition to form Lumps. They break up the information, grind it fine, and make it into bricks to build the story with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate necessary background/information by breaking it up: slip it into conversation, action-narration, passing reference, implication, or anywhere it won't feel 'lumpy.' Tell enough that readers understand the situation without making them feel lectured; make readers learn without realizing they're learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastic Lump exercise (invented background)
rubrics_metrics.description: Study this piece of false history and invented information till you're familiar with it. Then use it as the foundation of a story or a scene. As you write the scene, compost the information: break it up, spread it out, slip it into conversation or action-narration or anywhere you can make it go so it doesn't feel Lumpy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include enough of the invented information that readers unfamiliar with it can understand the scene (example: the queen imprisoned in a tower, politics of Harath). Aim for two or three pages; tell the info by implication, passing reference, or hint so the exposition feels part of the narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real Lump exercise (real procedural exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of something you know how to do that involves a complex series of specific actions (e.g., making bread, building a barn, designing a costume). It should be something that not everybody knows how to do, so most readers will want some explanation of the procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your knowledge plus sensory detail to keep the description vivid. Spread steps and explanatory information into the scene, so readers can follow without encountering an expository lump. Avoid overly complex industrial processes unless you already know them well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot vs story perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is merely one way of telling a story, by connecting the happenings tightly, usually through causal chains. A story that has nothing but action and plot is a pretty poor affair; and some great stories have neither. There are a limited number of plots... There is no limit to the number of stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't feel obliged to map out an elaborate tight plot before you write; if you are a planner, do so, but if you aren't, trust that a scene, character, place, or situation can lead you to a story. Think of 'steering the craft' as helping the story-boat find its own course; know in general where you're going but allow the telling to reveal the specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive passages can be narrative action
rubrics_metrics.description: All the examples quoted are fairly direct in their description, yet they do not slow or stop the story. The story is in the scene, in the things described. There's a tendency to fear descriptive 'passages,' as if they were unnecessary ornaments that inevitably slow the 'action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use description to carry information, mood, character, and movement. Well-crafted description (landscape, detailed setting) can be the action itself and should be woven into the narrative so it propels rather than retards the story. Look at examples across genres (memoir, thriller, fantasy) for models of integrating setting and information into narrative momentum.
